prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps) implements Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), following International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidance for National Airspace System (NAS) Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) operations. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)/airspace users negotiate assigned closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs), current-state-to-destination. Aircraft comply within tolerances and share predicted intent; controllers retain separation responsibility, without routine self-separation. Automation distributes changes to affected users, aircraft and FAA systems. NAS Constraint Service publishes static/dynamic constraints. Traffic management automation translates traffic management initiatives (TMIs) into traceable flight-specific constraints. Negotiating controllers subsume D-side duties; traffic management coordinators (TMCs) support traffic flow management (TFM).
TFM is separate: it selects TMIs; MBT assigns compliant trajectories, modifies them as constraints change, and supports constraint satisfaction. Improved predictability improves TMI selection. Near-term Ground Delay Programs (GDPs)/Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) remain unchanged; longer-term, Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) constraints at limited resources replace departure constraints using Expect Departure Clearance Time (EDCT).
Near-term mixed equipage uses System Wide Information Management (SWIM) extensions. Far-term Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2) supports digital trajectories and automatic/manual Flight Management System (FMS) loading; voice remains. Controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) exchanges clearances/intent. Required Time of Arrival (RTA) FMS supports one active RTA. Required Time Performance (RTP) certification is mandatory, even without RTA; RTP-Y specifies crossing-time-error 95% confidence interval in seconds, regardless of distribution, for TOAC constraints; complements Required Navigation Performance (RNP).
Surface MBT is excluded unless incremental benefits justify inclusion; ground operations remain separate research. TBO may control pushback from scheduled takeoff/runway queues without closed surface trajectories. MBT requires surface/en-route data exchange and assigned trajectories consistent with surface-management event predictions: reliable takeoff/landing times, runway assignments, departure/arrival transitions. Emergent users may use alternative sites; space vehicles may lack surface movement; rotorcraft air-taxi need neither taxiways nor runways.

New part:
U0101: The operator will have flexibility to determine when the aircraft takes off, depending on how fast or slow it wants to fly to conform with the CTA and how the takeoff time will affect other constraints.
U0102: Mile-in-trail and minute-in-trail (MINIT) restrictions will be reduced in the near term and eventually eliminated as unnecessary when flights are following 4DTs that include time-based constraints where necessary.
U0103: Increased use of self-separation techniques (e.g., A-IM) will allow efficient management of aircraft merging to a runway or other constrained airspace resource, without needing to repeatedly update time constraints in the assigned trajectories in response to residual uncertainty.
U0104: By keeping all flights on closed trajectories that are de-conflicted over at least the next 30 minutes, MBT may increase sector capacities.
U0105: Uncertainty, which MBT will reduce, hampers current TFM performance.
U0106: However, many TFM processes take advantage of the flexibility in current operations.
U0107: In any TBO environment, if aircraft are more predictable and are scheduled accordingly, the reduction in uncertainty may be accompanied by a reduction in flexibility.
U0108: However, some residual uncertainty will persist, creating the possibility that the TFM system might be more fragile to the remaining uncertainty.
U0109: One area in which research will be required to validate the MBT concept is how TFM must adjust to the tradeoff between uncertainty and flexibility to achieve the anticipated TFM benefits.
U0110: For example, if TFM continues to be conservative and initially absorb less delay than it expects will be required, to leave flexibility to fill an empty slot caused by another flight being late, then most flights will need their assigned trajectories to be updated, potentially multiple times, as the TFM system “releases” more and more of the expected necessary delay to the flights.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
